body: Seems like the `TrackType` enum causes issues with GHA & the extension API due to `TRACK_SIGNAL` shifting everything below it. I'm unsure if I should go the easy route and just move `TRACK_SIGNAL` to the end (which kind of feels _off_ for me due to how signals are consistently below methods in the implementation), or figuring out how to regenerate and apply a new extension api json 🤔

I wonder what the advantages of this over MethodTrack are. If there is no particular reason for the runtime to need this, I think it would be sufficient to simply add a helper function for the MethodTrack to the editor to list the signals and keying the emit_signal() function - like provide options such as “insert signal key” when right click keying or display a button in the inspector, etc., rather than adding a new TrackType needlessly.

> I wonder what the advantages of this over MethodTrack are. If there is no particular reason for the runtime to need this, I think it would be sufficient to simply add a helper function to the editor to list the signals and keying the emit_signal() function with MethodTrack, rather than adding a new TrackType needlessly.

There's quite a few reasons why I think a dedicated SignalTrack would be beneficial. Aside from the the obvious fact that they're easier to distinguish from each other, it also helps declutter the method track and clarify when a signal actually needs to be called, especially when signal emissions (via `emit_signal`) and function calls are tightly packed together. This track also eliminates that need to modify the MethodTrack in any way, since it allows the user to select a signal directly.

This way the design philosophy is clear and intuitive: Method tracks should exclusively be used for **methods**, and Signal tracks should exclusively be used for **signals**. I believe that this separation aligns with Godot’s emphasis on clarity and explicitness in its architecture.

Rather, it seems to diverge from Godot's design philosophy of object-orientation.

As you can see from the AnimationMixer code, the track type is determined by the processing for interpolation as a single unit. Since calling signal and method track are the same process, there must be into one TrackCache. This means that even if you add a SignalTrack by any chance, you must use the TrackCacheMethod for interpolation.

Considering that, if we add a SignalTrack, it may be that the SignalTrack should inherit MethodTrack.

However, in my opinion, adding one bool like is_signal to MethodTrack or MethodTrackKey and providing singnal-specific usability within MethodTrack is the safest way forward.

> Rather, it seems to diverge from Godot's design philosophy of object-orientation.

I'm pretty sure that having SignalTrack and MethodTrack as separate types is **entirely** consistent with object-oriented design. In fact, this is exactly what OOP encourages with "single responsibility."

And it this _were_ the case, why do we have separate tracks for 3D position, rotation, and scale in the AnimationPlayer, instead of just using the "property track" to transform? This is a genuine question, because my understanding is that they all resolve to modifying properties on a node. Is this not the same thing or am i lost here 😅?

> As you can see from the AnimationMixer code, the track type is determined by the processing for interpolation as a single unit. Since calling signal and method track are the same process, there must be into one TrackCache. This means that even if you add a SignalTrack by any chance, you must use the TrackCacheMethod for interpolation.

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by this. Method calls and signal emissions don’t really involve interpolation; there is no blending, easing, or tweening, they're discrete events. And if you're talking about _internal_ reuse of the TrackCacheMethod for handling discrete calls, then that's more of an argument for code reuse and clean implementation separation rather than having no SignalTrack.

> Considering that, if we add a SignalTrack, it may be that the SignalTrack should inherit MethodTrack.
>
> However, in my opinion, adding one bool like is_signal to MethodTrack and providing singnal-specific usability within MethodTrack is the safest way forward.

While this makes sense, I wouldn't really want to pollute the MethodTrack with dual responsibility, that seems like heading in the opposite direction of OOP design.

> And it this were the case, why do we have separate tracks for 3D position, rotation, and scale in the AnimationPlayer, instead of just using the "property track" to transform?

Position3D/Rotation3D/Scale3D/BlendShape were separated mainly for compression. You may refer to this article https://godotengine.org/article/animation-data-redesign-40/.

In interpolation, the processes for decompressing them and calculating the root motion are separated.

However, the caches for the Position3D/Rotation3D/Scale3D tracks are combined into one. In a more understandable example, BezierTrack and ValueTrack use the same TrackCache. You should first understand the AnimationMixer code flow.

> While this makes sense, I wouldn't really want to pollute the MethodTrack with dual responsibility, that seems like heading in the opposite direction of OOP design.

There are different ways to implement this depending on which units (per track or per key) you want to separate.

If anyone have an existing Method track, it seems tedious to go to the bother of adding a new Signal track when they want to add a signal to it. The opposite is also true.

I believe that there is no difference in responsibility between firing an external Node signal, i.e., calling the `emit_signal()` method, and calling another method. So, in my opinion, it should be sufficient if we could just determine if the key of the MethodTrack is "signal" or not. Then, it still be consistent that the responsibility of the Method track is only to call the method. The only difference is the data structure of the keys.

---

This is a bit off topic - If the SignalTrack is separate from the MethodTrack, currently, Animation cannot have two same tracks, so having Method and Signal in the same frame would seem to be an advantage. (The current workaround is to prepare a function that wraps multiple functions and call it on the method track.)

However, there is also the problem that the current Animation cannot easily reorder the tracks, this means that the order of the calls cannot be determined.

To solve this problem, I think we should allow the MethodTrack key to register multiple Methods.

In this case, if the SignalTrack is separate from the MethodTrack, duplicate implementations will be required.

However, if Signal is just a variation of a Key that MethodTrack has, it can be put in the same list.

---

In conclusion, I believe that SignalTrack should not be added and that having a bool called is_signal for MethodTrack's key is appropriate for future designs.

While I can totally see your point for dedicating the MethodTrack's functionality to better support signals, I still don't understand how having a dedicated track for signals is *less* intuitive in any way rather than grouping signals and methods on the same track. The separation makes it easier to read; the dedicated track makes adding signals intuitive (via a signal select panel); the tracks being separate encourages having tracks for *dedicated*, **single-purpose** keyframes; and the two separate tracks make the intent very clear, whereas coupling the two in a "method" track doesn't really convey to the user that they can or should call signals from the track.

> I believe that there is no difference in responsibility between firing an external Node signal, i.e., calling the emit_signal() method, and calling another method.

As I said above, this is what it is all about.

Think about why the AudioTrack and AnimationPlaybackTrack are separated from the MethodTrack. As you can see from the C++ code, it is because they not only call a specific Node's method, but also need to manage playback time, etc.

Conversely, the SignalTrack that you are adding here is synonymous in process with the MethodTrack that calls `emit_signal()`, and most of the code is duplicated on the AnimationMixer. So at least such duplication should be avoided.

> the dedicated track makes adding signals intuitive (via a signal select panel);

I agree with the addition of a signal selection panel. So displaying it in MethodTrack when adding inspectors and keys and keying for signals would be sufficient to show users how to use it.

If you feel that keys that `emit_signal()` methods and keys that call other methods are mixed in a row is a problem, you can consider adjusting the look by changing the color of only the keys for the emitting signal.

> the two separate tracks make the intent very clear, whereas coupling the two in a "method" track doesn't really convey to the user that they can or should call signals from the track.

While separating tracks for specific methods may be a fine thing for visual neatness, but I feel that we should not give special treatment to only the `emit_signal(`) method.

For example, there may be tracks where we want to call only methods such as `change_state()`, and we may want to separate them from MethodTrack. In this case, I think we should be able to separate any method, rather than treating only the method `emit_signal()` as a specific use.

So another idea as a compromise would be to allow subpaths to MethodTrack to bind the method to be called and only keying the arguments. This would satisfy your desire to separate only the `emit_signal()` method, and there is no need to separate SignalTrack from MethodTrack. - FYI, the ValueTrack with trackpath `Node:foo` in UpdateModeDiscrete is like a subpath MethodTrack with a `set_foo()` method bound to it as I suggested.

It may needs a special case (like string matching with subpath) but I assume you could make the signal selection panel appear there only when the MethodTrack have a subpath with `emit_signal()`.

> Think about why the AudioTrack and AnimationPlaybackTrack are separated from the MethodTrack. As you can see from the C++ code, it is because they not only call a specific Node's function, but also need to manage playback time, etc.

This misses the point i'm trying to make. These are separate not just because they manage time, but because they model different domains: audio playback, animation playback, and method calls are different concerns. By that same logic, Signal emission is separate from method invocation. Even if their execution is similar, their semantics and purpose differ,

> Conversely, the SignalTrack that you are adding here is synonymous in process with the MethodTrack that calls emit_signal(), and most of the code is duplicated on the AnimationMixer. So at least such duplication should be avoided.

Duplication in AnimationMixer is an argument for implementation, not an argument against separation. If this is a major concern, understand that duplicated code does not correspond with changing the implementation entirely. In fact, having these distinct also offers much more ease with maintainability: signal logic exists exclusively within _signal_ tracks, whereas the alternative requires digging through the increased complexity added to method logic.

> While separating tracks for specific methods may be a fine thing for visual neatness, but I feel that we should not give special treatment to only the emit_signal() method ... we should be able to separate any method, rather than treating only the method emit_signal() as a specific use.

Signals and methods are different, this should be given. Semantically, emitting a signal and calling a method are two different operations, `emit_signal()` just provides a functional bridge to emit these signals. There's also a difference in intent and behavior model. If there’s no difference, why does the engine distinguish them in every other system? Why not just call `emit_signal()` manually everywhere instead of connecting signals?

> Otherwise, we might as well allow any method (e.g., change_state()) to have its own track.

This is false equivalence and slippery slope; the reason `emit_signal()` is different is not arbitrary. It’s a well known part of Godots event system: **signals are meant to decouple logic**. A method like `change_state()` is user-defined. Emitting a signal is a fundamental construct of Godot, with a clear purpose and actual editor integration.

> So another idea as a compromise would be to allow subpaths to MethodTrack to bind the method to be called and only keying the arguments.

Now we're introducing hidden string based behavior to define editor UI behavior, which can be fragile, hard to debug, and likely against Godot’s insistence of explicitness.

If you need to introduce special casing and magic strings to emulate a feature, that's probably a strong sign that the feature deserves some abstraction.

This is something I have been wanting as someone who works with the animationplayer frequently. As someone who finds signals and methods in the same track unintuitive, this implementation makes complete sense to me.

> If there’s no difference, why does the engine distinguish them in every other system? Why not just call emit_signal() manually everywhere instead of connecting signals?

The cases where signals and methods need to be separated are the Class itself which has signals to register in the ClassDB, and the Node which connects to the signals to subscribe to them. Since AnimationMixer is neither of those cases and be an entity external to the target Node, so there is no difference between calling `emit_signal()` method and calling another method from the outside of the target Node.

> > If there’s no difference, why does the engine distinguish them in every other system? Why not just call emit_signal() manually everywhere instead of connecting signals?
> 
> The cases where signals and methods need to be separated are the Class itself which has signals to register in the ClassDB, and the Node which connects to the signals to subscribe to them. Since AnimationMixer is neither of those cases and be an entity external to the target Node, so there is no difference between calling `emit_signal()` method and calling another method from the outside of the target Node.

Once again, signals and methods are semantically different, where methods are imperative (do this) and signal emissions are declarative (this happened). That difference exists regardless of who initiates the call. Because of this difference, users _think_ about them differently, so the editor should continue to reflect that as it already has been. Even if both actions reduced to call() under the hood, they serve different architectural purposes, and the UX should make that explicit rather than hiding it behind a special case in the MethodTrack.
If we can emulate signals under methods calls we should because of how burdensome adding a new track is done and like making the entire engine aware of this

> Once again, signals and methods are semantically different, where methods are imperative (do this) and signal emissions are declarative (this happened).

This is about the signal from the point of view of the node which has that signal, not about the signal of the target node from the point of view of the AnimationMixer. From the AnimationMixer's point of view, it is still only a process of calling an `emit_signal()`.

I am not opposed to extending AnimationEditor for signals, but the internal implementation of AnimationMixer should not make a special distinction between `emit_signal()` method and any other methods.

> If we can emulate signals under methods calls we should because of how burdensome adding a new track is done and like making the entire engine aware of this

Emulating signals through `emit_signal()` in MethodTrack puts the onus on the user to know that (first) this is possible, and (second) how to do it. It hides a first-class engine concept (signals) behind an opaque method call, which goes against Godot’s general philosophy of **explicitness over magic**. Yes, I know that the method track can be adjusted for this, but this feels like you're bloating the method track and straying away from the OOP principle of individual responsibities. And when you mean adding a track is burdensome, are you talking about for the end user or internally? For the end user, it is literally just one menu you have to open. If you're talking about internal implementation, it's kind of already done, and I'll reiterate what I said before: having separate logic for signals is almost always better for maintainability than adding _even more_ complexity to method logic. Admittedly yeah, it is true that the logic for the signal track can be changed to better optimize emission, but that is an _implementation issue_, not an argument against a signal track.

> This is about the signal from the point of view of the node which has that signal, not about the signal of the target node from the point of view of the AnimationMixer. From the AnimationMixer's point of view, it is still only a process of calling an emit_signal().
>
> I am not opposed to extending AnimationEditor for signals, but the internal implementation of AnimationMixer should not make a special distinction between emit_signal() method and any other methods.

You're totally right that from the AnimationMixer's internal perspective (at the ground level) emitting a signal via `emit_signal()` level is just a method call. But externally, this is **exactly** the reason to distinguish these at the track and editor level: because what is semantically identical within the _engine_ doesn't have to be conflated in the UI or API. One thing that should be considered is that the user’s mental model isn’t the same as the engine’s call stack, that’s where clarity, intent, and usability come into play.

---

To put it simply: `emit_signal()` is not a conventional builtin method, that should be obvious. No logic is performed, only the emission of the signal. The actual logic is carried by the *listeners* of the signal, which in my opinion is a big enough distinction on its own for having signal emissions and methods on separate tracks. Regardless, all `emit_signal()` does is bridge the dispatching of signals to the end user; it simply just boils down to whether the signals (broadcast communication) and methods (direct logic) are different enough to merit having separate tracks. I believe that this _is_ the case, where keeping signals in their own track separates *event emissions* from other standard logic, making animations easier to organize and maintain whilst also following closely with the principles aforementioned.
Closing this. Since emit_signal() works well enough I won’t argue against it
